narrative:
Short impact summary

An Introduction to Statistical Learning has become a major reference point in statistical learning and machine learning, with 11,921 OpenAlex citations and top 1% standing for its field and year. Its influence is also visible in public and teaching-facing contexts, including Wikipedia mentions, library holdings, and a small but clear sign of instructional reuse.

Full narrative

Published by Springer Nature in 2013 as part of the Springer Texts in Statistics series, An Introduction to Statistical Learning by Gareth James, Daniela Witten, Trevor Hastie, and Robert Tibshirani has accumulated substantial scholarly uptake across statistics, computer science, mathematics education, artificial intelligence, and adjacent applied fields. The citation record is especially strong: 11,921 OpenAlex citations places the book in the top 1% of works for its field and year, indicating sustained and wide-ranging use as a foundational source rather than a narrowly specialized text.

The citing landscape shows that the book is being used broadly across publication types and venues, with articles dominating but also many conference papers, preprints, book chapters, and dissertations. That pattern is consistent with a work that functions as a shared methodological baseline for both research and teaching. The most visible topical links in the citing record cluster around statistical methods and inference, machine learning and data classification, anomaly detection, forecasting, and other applied analytics areas, suggesting that the book serves as a common methodological reference across diverse problem domains.

Public and community-facing signals reinforce that role. The book appears in Wikipedia-related attention, and it is linked in a small amount of broader online discussion outside formal citation channels. Reader-reception sources such as LibraryThing, Google Books, Amazon, and Goodreads also indicate continued visibility among general and scholarly readers. While these signals do not measure academic influence directly, they do show that the book remains present in public knowledge spaces and in commercial and reader-oriented ecosystems.

There is also evidence of adoption in teaching and reference environments. Library holdings are recorded in WorldCat and Open Library, and the book appears in a YouTube item that explicitly links it in the video metadata or description, which is a modest but concrete sign of instructional or explanatory use. Scite records further show that most citation statements are supporting or merely mentioning, with only a very small number contradicting, indicating that the book is largely cited as a credible and usable source within the literature. Overall, the record portrays a highly influential textbook that continues to anchor statistical learning practice in research, education, and public-facing explanation.
